title: Greetings & Politeness
description: Hello at every time of day, thank you and sorry, goodbye, and how to address people with Bapak, Ibu, Mas and Mbak. The words you'll use every day, with anyone.

phrases.registerNotes: From early morning until about 11 a.m. The reply is the same: Selamat pagi, or just Pagi.
From about 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., the hottest part of the day.
phrases.pitfallNote: Siang is midday, not afternoon. English speakers switch to selamat sore after noon, but at 1 p.m. it's still siang.

phrases.registerNotes: From about 3 p.m. until it gets dark, which near the equator is around 6 p.m. all year.
After dark, both when you arrive and when you leave. Going to bed, it's selamat tidur.
Dropping selamat is warm and everyday, with neighbours, staff and colleagues; Siang, Pak and Sore, Bu work the same way.
phrases.cultureNote: Bapak (Pak) and Ibu (Bu) mean father and mother, and they're how you address any adult older than you or in a formal role: shopkeepers, drivers, officials. Adding one is the quickest way to sound polite.

phrases.registerNotes: Literally 'what news?'. For people you know or are meeting properly; with someone older, add the title: Apa kabar, Pak?
phrases.pitfallNote: It isn't a passing 'how's it going?': you don't say it to a cashier. Neighbours in the street greet with Mau ke mana? instead.

phrases.registerNotes: The usual answer to Apa kabar?; Kabar baik ('the news is good') is the fuller form. To ask back, add Bapak sendiri bagaimana? or Ibu sendiri bagaimana? (And yourself?).
Right everywhere, with anyone. Terima kasih banyak is thank you very much; makasih is the casual clipped form.
The everyday reply to terima kasih, to anyone. You may also hear Kembali ('back to you'), which is a little more formal.
For apologising, and to soften a question or a correction: Maaf, boleh tanya? (Sorry, can I ask something?). Mohon maaf is the formal version.
phrases.pitfallNote: To squeeze past someone or catch a waiter's eye, the word is permisi. Maaf is for when you've done something wrong or are about to impose.

phrases.registerNotes: To get someone's attention, to get past, or to announce yourself at a door or a shop. Also said as you leave: Permisi, Bu.
phrases.cultureNote: When walking in front of people who are sitting down, people stoop a little and hold the right arm low as they say permisi.

phrases.registerNotes: Tolong ('help') goes before the verb to ask someone to do something for you; ya at the end softens it. Add Pak or Bu to be more polite still.
phrases.pitfallNote: Tolong comes first, not last like English 'please'. Shouted on its own, Tolong means 'Help'.

phrases.registerNotes: Offering or inviting: letting someone go first, take a seat or start eating. As a guest you'll hear Silakan masuk (come in) and Silakan duduk (have a seat).
phrases.pitfallNote: Silakan invites someone to do something for themselves; tolong asks them to do something for you. It's spelt silakan, though silahkan is common on signs.

phrases.english: Please, help yourself. (said when you're eating)
phrases.registerNotes: Mari is a polite 'let's'; in casual speech it's ayo. On its own, Mari, Pak is also a polite goodbye as you walk on.
phrases.cultureNote: If someone comes by while you're eating, it's polite to offer with Mari makan. It's a courtesy, not a real invitation, and the answer is usually Silakan, silakan (go ahead).

phrases.registerNotes: Put your own name in. More formally, start with Perkenalkan ('let me introduce myself'): Perkenalkan, nama saya Emma.
phrases.pitfallNote: There's no 'is', and the owner comes after the thing: nama saya is literally 'name my'.

phrases.registerNotes: Namanya ('the name') neatly avoids choosing a word for 'you'. To someone older, Nama Bapak siapa? or Nama Ibu siapa?
phrases.pitfallNote: A name is asked with siapa (who), not apa (what).

phrases.registerNotes: Polite and safe at a first meeting. To someone older, swap Anda for Bapak or Ibu: Senang bertemu dengan Ibu.
phrases.pitfallNote: Anda is polite but a little impersonal face to face; Indonesians usually say the person's name or Bapak or Ibu instead.

phrases.english: Nice to meet you. (when introducing yourself)
phrases.registerNotes: Literally 'greetings of acquaintance'. Said after your name, especially to a group or in a first message; friendly but still polite.
Add the title to thank anyone who serves you: Terima kasih, Pak / Bu / Mas / Mbak. On its own, terima kasih is fine too.
phrases.cultureNote: Mas (to a young man) and Mbak (to a young woman) are how people in Jakarta and Java address waiters, shop staff and drivers around their own age; Pak and Bu are for anyone older. Elsewhere, Kak is a safe, friendly choice.

phrases.registerNotes: Iya means the same, a little softer, and is very common in speech. At the end of a sentence, ya softens it, like 'OK?'.
phrases.pitfallNote: Ya often means 'I'm listening' rather than 'I agree'. Nodding along with ya can sound like you've agreed to something.

phrases.registerNotes: For turning down an offer from a vendor or a driver, with a smile. Tidak usah, terima kasih ('no need') is just as common.
phrases.pitfallNote: Tidak says no to doing or being something. To say 'no, it's not that thing', use bukan: Ini kopi? Bukan, ini teh.

phrases.registerNotes: The all-purpose goodbye. Sampai jumpa lagi is see you again, sampai besok is see you tomorrow, and with friends it's sampai ketemu.
With a wave, to friends and children. Not to anyone you'd call Bapak or Ibu.
The polite way to leave a house, a shop or a meeting. Dulu ('first') makes it gentle. With friends, it's Aku duluan, ya.
phrases.cultureNote: People rarely just slip away: telling the host, and anyone older, that you're leaving is expected.

phrases.registerNotes: Said to the person who is leaving: at a station, an airport or the end of a visit. Literally 'safe journey'.
Said by the person leaving to those who stay. Literally 'safe staying'.
phrases.pitfallNote: It sounds final, like a farewell for a long time. For an everyday goodbye, say Saya permisi dulu or Sampai jumpa.
